title: Hossenshiki Ceremony
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Edie shares that true freedom and direction can be found in embracing our imperfections and letting go of attachments, rather than trying to achieve some idealized state. By cultivating discernment and living with openness and humility, we can tap into our true nature and find peace in the midst of uncertainty and chaos. This approach requires us to practice non-thinking and acceptance, rather than trying to control or manipulate our experiences.

sentences.text: *Xiaozhou asked Nanquan, "What is the way?"
Nanquan said, "Everyday mind."
Xiaozhou said, "How should I direct myself toward it?"
Nanquan replied, "If you direct yourself toward it, you will be going in the wrong direction."
Xiaozhou said, "But if I don't direct myself toward it, how can I know it?"
Nanquan said, "The way has nothing to do with knowing and not knowing.
Knowing is an exaggeration, not knowing is stupidity.
When you enter the way, you see it is vast, as vast and boundless as space.
What does this have to do with yes and no thinking?"
Xiaozhou suddenly realized Nanquan's meaning for himself.*
*This is the Dharma staff, five feet long.
Once a black snake on Vulture Peak, it became the Udumbara flower.
At Shaolin Temple, it burst forth the five petals of Zen.
This is now in my hands.
Sometimes it is a dragon swallowing heaven and earth, sometimes a Vajra sword giving and taking life.
It is now in my hands.
Though only a mosquito biting an iron bulb, I cannot give it away.
Dragons and elephants, let us call forth the Dharma.
Give me your questions.*
Shuso, how can I remember?
Say hello.
Shuso, how can I really welcome each?
Smile.
Shuso, I'm very attached to those I love, but one day they will have to die.
How can I accept?
Don't linger.
I practice with just enough.
During your initiation ceremony, people refer to you as the wise matriarch of the Sangha.
What has a wise matriarch learned from being Shuso?
Run after them.
Shuso, how does one become a worthy clan elder?
Beats me.
One practices renunciation.
That's the best time to renounce, because you can't do anything else but.
Shuso, do you have any words of wisdom for myself, who has just had her 70th birthday?
Look forward to many more.
Shuso, when I'm home alone and my thoughts are distracted, how can I be more in my body?
Feel your belly and breathe into it, and your mind will go right there.
Shuso, yesterday the birds were singing.
Today the sun is shining.
The tree next door is blossoming.
Is it spring?
I think so.
Shuso, in your classes we looked at poetry.
I often think of myself as the monkey hanging from Master Hakuen.
The branch breaks of its own accord.
Does the monkey still enter the way?
Or must the monkey let go of its own will?
There's no letting go.
There's no will.
There's no branch.
There's no monkey.
Shuso, I'm wondering.
Do what you're facing.
Do that and then face another direction and do that.
Shuso, [unclear: "a woman mad"].
Everyone's gender holds oneself and asserts itself at different times, in different ways.
Shuso, on renouncing, [unclear: "played"] the lesson of the two cats.
With the new cat jumping, let them fight it out.
Shuso, a talk yesterday alluded to the impermanence of the self.
Who is it that does the renouncing?
Good point.
At the beginning of your Dharma talk, you said you left out the part about sex.
Tell us about it.
Sex!
Shuso, you also said, sitting quietly we gain nothing.
We go nowhere.
Explain quietly.
You spoke yesterday of self and non-self.
How best to practice non-self?
Non-thinking.
Shuso, if I understood correctly, you equated resignation with a kind of acceptance.
How do you know when to act to change what's in front of you, or when to just accept what is?
I don't think I said resignation.
I said renunciation.
Really different.
So can you ask your question again?
I got caught on that one.
If renunciation is accepting whatever comes up, how do you know when to act?
Because sometimes what comes up is bad.
Discernment is important.
Reflection.
Shuso, I'm very disturbed by what's happening in the world and how inhumanely human beings treat one another, by my own confusion.
And sometimes I lose faith in Buddha nature.
And I wonder why religions have been trying to help us to manifest that part of ourselves for thousands of years.
Why is it so hard?
They're teaching the wrong thing, I think.
Shuso, how do you live with loneliness?
Enjoy it.
With creativity, feeling renewed, but I know, what should I think of?
Fades.
Think of the next great idea.
Shuso, we live in a world torn apart by conflict and crisis.
And I work in a workplace of conflict and crisis.
How do I not get torn apart?
Live in but not of, or of but not in, whichever way works.
Shuso, my sister has a very severe spinal curvature.
It began when she was five years old.
Still now, I feel guilt in my own nice body.
And my mother has pain that she couldn't fix.
How can I be with these, my mother's pain and my guilt?
All are gifts to each of us.
Shuso, I just arrived this morning.
What have I missed?
Not a thing.
Shuso, you spoke so clearly and so deeply about renunciation.
I ask you, what direction can we turn in despair?
To the truth of suffering?
Shuso, can you give me some advice to help me practice?
Don't say much.
Shuso, somehow I feel that women's deepest stories and koans didn't make it into the collections.
What is your life koan?
Relinquishing.
Shuso, I've accomplished so many things I set out to accomplish, and I feel like an absolute failure.
What have I done wrong?
Nothing.
You're halfway there.
Do you really practice humility?
Look in the mirror.
This has been a wonderful retreat and practice period, and your questions have been riveting to me.
I appreciate them all and all of your friendship.

I told Norman before we came in the room that I wanted to dedicate this ceremony to my deceased parents, long deceased, to my sisters, one of whom is deceased, to my two sons and their families, four grandchildren.
Nobody ever expected any of this.
Through the support of the lineage, the teacher, and all of you, I have been Shuso.
I am deeply grateful for your help, but I have not been worthy of it.
Friends, if my words or deeds have misled you, please wash out your ears in the Dharma's harmonious silence, the silence that is within all sound, within and without.
And please keep on practicing, as I will.
Let us practice together through this lifetime and into the next, perfect in our imperfections.
Thank you very much.
[unclear: "Tings have been enjoyed"].
From the Seattle [unclear: "Sado Zen"].
We haven't met, I think, in your teaching.
You're from the Shusos.
Now you're in a big club.
Congratulations, and thank you so much for sharing your teaching, sharing your knowledge and your wisdom.
And thank you for sharing your duties as Shuso with the Vancouver Sangha and helping to continue to weave the wonderful threads that bind us together as sister sanghas.
I would say that I hope you feel the same warmth and openness of heart that I felt when I was finishing my task as Shuso, but I think you already had that.
I feel such wonderful warmth from you and I feel really grateful that I was able to host you and get to know you better.
It's been a real gift to me.
Thank you very much.
Edie, congratulations.
Thank you for your courage, and especially for your Dharma talk yesterday.
There's a line that you said so eloquently about, I think it's when the mind is looking for renunciation, but then it comes from the heart.
Edie, really fortunate that I was able to hear your Way Seeking Mind talk in January, and the teachings of that talk and knowing you a little bit better through that talk are still effective.
So thank you very much for that, and it's such a thrill to at least be able to be here for this ceremony.
Edie, I'll say thank you, but to also say this is not the end.
This is the beginning.
Thank you more for your words of wisdom and just sharing life and the Dharma with you.
We really are one family.
Edie, whenever you have stepped forward with a talk or a class, your deep practice and life experience just shines through.
It's been a wonderful six weeks to have more of that.
I'm really grateful to you for that and I look forward to practicing for many years.

Edie, as I enter my years of [unclear: "Chromehood"], it's been really inspiring to have an older sister for a while and I hope to continue to appreciate so much your courage and humor and clarity and inspiration.
So onwards and grannies.
What have we got to lose?

Thank you for all the wonderful work you've done, much of which I missed of course because I was sick, but it was wonderful and I know it could be there, and I think I have a lot to learn from you about grace, being concise, and being wise.
I look forward to learning more from you.
Eight years ago we first performed a ceremony in the Northwest and you were sitting in the audience and you asked the question, how can I be a monk in the world?
So I think we're seeing the beginning of the answer and I'm really looking forward to the next installment that's really going to help all of us in the whole world.
So please keep asking the questions.
How wonderful.
What a pleasure.
What a deep pleasure to sit in the midst of all this Dharma and beauty.
Zen Rin Shinge, that's Edie's name.
It was given to her by Tenshin Anderson, a very perceptive guy, because the name means sitting lotus profound wisdom.
Isn't that the perfect name for Edie?
She, in this retreat and all the time that she's been in Shuso, has been occupying her seat just like a lotus flower, a beautiful beauty in muddy water.
That's a lotus, right?
It grows out of the mud, all the trouble of the human body as it ages and it creaks and it groans and it grunts, and all the trouble to be a human being, so difficult, so muddy and so beautiful.
And we've seen today, and not only today, Edie's profound wisdom.
And you know what the best part of this is for me?
She has no idea.
Isn't that great?
She has no idea.
So this is what we should all aspire to, right?
To manifest profound wisdom and have no idea that we're doing it, none whatsoever, just to say, what?
I don't know, but I'll try.
What a great spirit, it lies at the exact center of our tradition.
Beautiful, beautiful questions today, right from the heart, real questions, real human concerns.
And who would have guessed that Zenrin Shinge would be the master of the one word answer, or even, when the occasion demands, the no word.
So that was really a treat.
I think sometimes we were left hanging.
We're still hanging, and isn't that how it is in life, still hanging until we drop out of that tree.
And I couldn't agree more with our Dharma leaders over here, many of whom said this is the beginning.
It really is the beginning once we go through the gate of Shuso and our heart is broken open.
We have to continue, there's no other way.
So I too look forward to the many ways in which Edie's profound wisdom continues to manifest in our community as she joins the wonderful ranks of our elders.
So I'm so grateful and so happy to be a part of this, my life's answer.
We practice pretty quietly.
It's a good secret, no one even knows we're here, but we have big ambitions, big ambitions.
We don't want this suffering of the world to continue and we are absolutely determined that it will end someday.
And we are making effort in that direction and we are confident that we're going to get there.
Probably not us in the room, we'll be gone, but that's okay because we're all of us together going to get there.
And so this beautiful practice period comes to a close.
Lots of people put out lots of effort to make it happen, creating a Dharma realm in the middle of the earth just by our efforts.

So thanks to everyone who made that happen, and let's dedicate all the positive energy in the practice period, of this retreat and of today's ceremony, as one more drop in the bucket that we're filling up little by little, the bucket of goodness, that when it spills over and floods the world, maybe we can call upon the worthy serving crew, one more coffee with cups and bowls.
The cooks might be able to advise you about what the food is, and we'll need to move the table out.
In the meantime we can just mill around and relax, and if you're not on that crew, stay up the stairs because there will be a lot of traffic.
There'll be a few minutes more cooking.
Okay, a few minutes, please relax, we'll enjoy the food.
